items.explanation: The Dawes Act broke reservations into 160/80/40-acre individual allotments, with 'surplus' land sold to white settlers. Its explicit aim was assimilation: dissolve tribal landholding and communal life and remake Native people as individual, property-owning Christian farmers. It cost tribes ~90 million acres.
options: (A) To dissolve tribal landholding and remake Native peoples as individual farmers.
(B) To preserve and sustain Native languages and traditional cultural practices.
(C) To open Native lands in Georgia, South Carolina, and Alabama to mining and cotton planters.
(D) To pay tribes financial compensation for lands seized through fraudulent treaties.
items.stem: A primary goal of the Dawes Severalty Act was which of the following?
items.stimulus: "...the President of the United States [is] hereby... authorized, whenever in his opinion any reservation or any part thereof of such Indians is advantageous for agricultural and grazing purposes, to cause said reservation... to be surveyed... and to allot the lands in said reservation in severalty [separate plots of land, individually owned] to any Indian located thereon..." — Dawes Severalty Act (excerpt), 1887

items.explanation: Jackson's A Century of Dishonor (1881) documented federal betrayals of treaties; she mailed a copy to every member of Congress. The moral pressure from such 'friends of the Indian' reformers helped produce the allotment policy.
options: (A) The Supreme Court's ruling in Worcester v. Georgia.
(B) A mass nonviolent protest movement against federal policy led by Crazy Horse.
(C) The Freedmen's Bureau's record of aiding formerly enslaved people in the South.
(D) Helen Hunt Jackson's A Century of Dishonor exposed federal mistreatment.
items.stem: An important impetus for the Dawes Act was which of the following?

items.explanation: Off-reservation boarding schools (e.g., Carlisle) cut children's hair, banned Native languages, imposed English names and vocational training — the same assimilationist logic as allotment: erase tribal identity by remaking the individual. The Indian Reorganization Act (1934) reversed this; AIM (1968) opposed it.
options: (A) The Ghost Dance movement's spiritual revival.
(B) The federal Indian boarding schools that erased Native languages.
(C) The Indian Reorganization Act's restoration of tribal governments.
(D) The American Indian Movement's 1960s activism.
items.stem: Which of the following shared the Dawes Act's underlying goal for the future of Native peoples?

items.explanation: The 1873 cartoon shows a Granger waking figures sleeping on railroad 'sleepers' (ties) as a locomotive labeled 'Consolidation Train,' 'extortion,' and 'bribery' bears down — the Grange warning farmers that unregulated railroad corporations threatened their livelihoods and the republic itself.
options: (A) Railroads were bringing prosperity to formerly isolated farming communities.
(B) Railroad corporations were neglecting the safety of their own workers.
(C) Americans needed to wake up to the danger giant railroad monopolies posed.
(D) Rail lines were corrupting rural culture by importing urban vices.
items.stem: [Image description: 'The Grange Awakening the Sleepers,' 1873 political cartoon. Figures sleep on railroad tracks (the crossbeams are called 'sleepers') while a standing Granger tries to rouse them; a locomotive rushes toward them with cars labeled 'Consolidation Train,' 'extortion,' 'bribery,' and similar terms.] The cartoon's main point is which of the following?

items.explanation: The National Grange of the Order of Patrons of Husbandry (founded 1867) organized farmers — first for mutual aid and better techniques, then for state railroad regulation (the Granger Laws) and cooperatives that bypassed middlemen.
options: (A) Farmers in the Midwest and West.
(B) Urban immigrant workers.
(C) Wealthy industrialists.
(D) Middle-class corporate managers.
items.stem: The Grange drew its strongest support from which group?

items.explanation: Farmers faced falling crop prices, high railroad freight rates, expensive credit, and grain-elevator monopolies while corporations amassed unprecedented economic and political power — the grievances that made the Grange a political force.
options: (A) The wave of Irish immigration after the 1840s potato famine.
(B) The concentration of economic power in giant corporations.
(C) The rise of urban political machines.
(D) Corporate campaigns to control markets in Asia and Latin America.
items.stem: The Grange emerged most directly in response to which nineteenth-century development?

items.explanation: The Populist (People's) Party of the 1890s absorbed the Granger program — railroad regulation, an income tax, free coinage of silver, subtreasury farm loans — and carried it into national politics with the 1892 Omaha Platform.
options: (A) The Congress of Industrial Organizations' labor organizing.
(B) The Populist Party's 1890s farmer-labor platform.
(C) The NAACP's civil-rights litigation strategy.
(D) The 1960s New Left student movement.
items.stem: Which later movement most fully carried forward the Grange's political and economic agenda?

items.explanation: Unlike most nativist cartoons of the era, Opper's is sympathetic: it parallels the Pilgrims' seventeenth-century hardships with the gauntlet facing 1880s immigrants — swindling money-changers, baggage thieves, slum landlords, and exploitative employers.
options: (A) The 'new immigrants' of eastern and southern Europe were as dangerous to America as Native peoples had been to the Pilgrims.
(B) America was filling up, and new immigrants would displace native-born Americans just as the Pilgrims displaced Native peoples.
(C) The immigrant stream contained radicals, anarchists, and criminals who threatened the nation.
(D) Newly arrived immigrants faced a gauntlet of exploitation and hardship, just as the Pilgrims had in the 1600s.
items.stem: [Image description: Frederick Burr Opper, 'Just as dangerous now as then,' 1883. A cartoon drawing a parallel between the perils the Pilgrims faced arriving in seventeenth-century America and the perils facing immigrants arriving in the 1880s.] The cartoon's point is which of the following?

items.explanation: Both the cartoon and the settlement-house movement (Hull House, 1889, founded by Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr) expressed sympathy for immigrants' plight and offered practical aid — a continuity of pro-immigrant sentiment against the era's nativism (Know-Nothings, Palmer Raids, 1924 quotas).
options: (A) Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr founding Hull House (1889) to aid immigrants.
(B) The Know-Nothing Party's 1854 anti-immigrant platform.
(C) Attorney General Palmer's deportation raids during the 1920s Red Scare.
(D) The Johnson-Reed Immigration Act of 1924 establishing discriminatory national-origins quotas.
items.stem: Which of the following best represents a continuity with the sentiment expressed in the Opper cartoon?

items.explanation: Rice describes Standard Oil underselling him by 1–3 cents a gallon because railroads gave it secret rebates — Rockefeller's horizontal integration: buying or crushing rival refiners to dominate one industry (oil refining), organized through the trust device.
options: (A) Global distribution networks.
(B) Horizontal integration: dominating a single industry by absorbing rivals.
(C) Regional economic planning.
(D) Vertical consolidation of the supply chain from raw materials to finished goods.
items.stem: The business strategy Rice describes is best classified as which of the following?
items.stimulus: "I am but one of many victims of Rockefeller's colossal combination.... I established what was known as the Ohio Oil Works.... I found... that the Standard Oil Company was offering the same quality of oil at much lower prices than I could do — from one to three cents a gallon less than I could possibly sell it for. I sought for the reason and found that the railroads were in league with the Standard Oil concern at every point, giving it discriminating rates and privileges of all kinds as against myself and all outside competitors." — George Rice, 'How I Was Ruined by Rockefeller,' New York World, October 16, 1898

items.explanation: Reformers passed the Sherman Antitrust Act (1890), but in U.S. v. E.C. Knight (1895) the Court confined it to interstate 'trade,' exempting manufacturing — leaving the sugar trust (98% of refining) untouched and blunting federal antitrust power for a generation.
options: (A) Congress passed antitrust laws but presidents routinely vetoed them.
(B) Reformers, politicians, and labor leaders quickly succeeded in restructuring the economy.
(C) Most Americans rejected antitrust efforts as communistic and un-American.
(D) Supreme Court rulings narrowed antitrust law, shielding manufacturers from regulation.
items.stem: Efforts to curb corporate power in the 1890s and 1900s were most significantly limited by which of the following?

items.explanation: Social Darwinism — Herbert Spencer's 'survival of the fittest' applied to society, popularized in the U.S. by William Graham Sumner — taught that great fortunes reflected natural superiority and that regulation would interfere with progress: the standard intellectual defense of laissez-faire industrialism.
options: (A) Herbert Spencer's Social Darwinism, which cast great wealth as fitness.
(B) Henry George's proposal for a single tax on land values.
(C) The Populist Omaha Platform's demands for government intervention.
(D) Upton Sinclair's The Jungle and its expose of the meatpacking industry.
items.stem: Defenders of the corporate practices Rice describes would most likely have appealed to which of the following?
